status: cross-era evaluation-protocol tension; direct replication needed
claim: Safety conclusions depend on seed inclusion, evaluation phase, and the selected safety metric. AI Safety Gridworlds (2017) trained 20 seeds and removed the worst 25% for its plotted averages; SafeRLEval (2026) retained 30 seeds and separately evaluated training policies with exploration noise and final greedy policies using mean cost, violation rate, violation magnitude, and cost distribution. It found that noisy-training and final-greedy safety can differ, and its FOCOPS versus PPO-Lag tier assignment changes relative to violation-rate ordering because tiering also requires average normalized cost deviation to be non-positive.

interpretation: The papers differ in environments, algorithms, and aims; this is not a direct replication and does not establish that the 2017 study is invalid. It identifies a protocol-sensitive distinction between typical performance and tail reliability that can be tested on matched runs.
falsifiable_question: On safe-RL benchmarks with complete seed-level logs, does excluding the worst quartile alter algorithm rankings or safety-threshold decisions relative to reporting every seed, and do rankings further change when evaluation switches from training-time exploration to final greedy execution?
primary_outcome: All-seed algorithm ordering and threshold classification under mean cost, violation probability, conditional violation magnitude, and tail-risk metrics, reported separately for training and final greedy policies.
counterevidence_and_caveats: AI Safety Gridworlds removed low-return runs to reduce variance; its purpose was not to estimate a deployed policy's tail risk.
The 2017 and 2026 studies use different environments and algorithms and cannot be numerically compared.
SafeRLEval is limited to four navigation tasks, three safety bounds, and algorithms that may violate constraints during training.
suggested_design: Re-run selected safe-RL baselines on common tasks with a preregistered full seed set; publish raw per-seed and per-episode costs; compare full-seed and trimmed-seed summaries only as a sensitivity analysis; evaluate both exploration-on training checkpoints and final greedy policies; report mean, violation rate, conditional overshoot, and tail quantiles with confidence intervals.
